overview: Savor Limited, established in 2011 and NZX-listed since 2012, is one of New Zealand's largest hospitality groups, operating approximately 18 food, beverage and entertainment venues concentrated in Auckland's Britomart, Wynyard Quarter, Ponsonby, Parnell and Mission Bay precincts. Its portfolio spans premium bar-and-restaurant brands (Amano, two Azabu venues, Ebisu, Bivacco Bar & Griglia, Non Solo Pizza, MoVida, Bar Ziti) alongside the fast-casual Oji sushi concept and, since September 2025, an entertainment-led golf-simulator venue (Flush Golf). The company positions itself as 'approachable premium' and is 100% exposed to a single city and to discretionary consumer spending on dining out.

business_model.summary: Savor makes money almost entirely from on-premise food and beverage sales at company-operated venues, recognised at point of sale, supplemented by private events/functions (deposits recognised on the event date) and a small wholesale/grab-and-go channel (Oji). Revenue is transactional and highly seasonal rather than recurring — roughly 65% of Group earnings are historically generated in the summer trading months (Nov-Mar), making the business acutely sensitive to a handful of months of weather, tourism and consumer sentiment. FY26 revenue was $55.2m (FY25: $56.6m, FY24: $61.9m), split across Hospitality as effectively the Group's sole reportable segment; Corporate costs are carried separately and are not a segment under NZ IFRS 8.

revenue_streams.name: Food & beverage (dine-in venues)
revenue_streams.trend: stable/declining like-for-like, offset by new venues

revenue_streams.name: Events, functions & catering
revenue_streams.trend: recovering as corporate events return to the CBD

revenue_streams.name: Entertainment (Flush Golf simulator bays)
revenue_streams.trend: growing - new format, trading ahead of expectation

revenue_streams.name: Wholesale / grab-and-go (Oji)
revenue_streams.trend: small, historically de-emphasised versus FY2022 ambitions

business_model.customer_type: B2C (walk-in diners, drinkers) with a B2B/private-events overlay (corporate functions, weddings); no subscription or contracted recurring revenue
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% Auckland, New Zealand - Britomart, Wynyard Quarter, Ponsonby, Parnell and Mission Bay precincts only; no offshore or other-city exposure

main_competitors: Independent single-site Auckland restaurateurs and chef-led venues
Hospitality group operators (e.g. Hip Group, Hancock & Monk / Cassia stable, Ostro-style independents)
International QSR and casual dining chains for discretionary spend (competing indirectly for the same wallet)
Hotel F&B outlets in the same precincts (Hilton, Sofitel, Park Hyatt, M Social)
Entertainment/social-format venues (mini-golf, bowling, other simulator/experiential concepts) for Flush Golf
competitive_position.market_position: One of the largest multi-venue hospitality operators in Auckland by venue count and revenue, but restaurants/bars remain a structurally fragmented, low-barrier-to-entry industry with no player commanding meaningful national market share; Savor's scale advantage is real but modest in absolute terms (~$55m revenue, ~$13m market cap).

moat_factors.description: Long-standing positions in Britomart and Wynyard Quarter, both under active landlord curation, are hard to replicate quickly; the 2025 Seafarers lease renewal to a more sustainable structure shows some negotiating leverage from tenure and scale.

Multiple distinct concepts (Japanese, Italian, Spanish tapas, entertainment) reduce single-brand fatigue risk and let the Group refresh underperforming sites without abandoning the group relationship with a landlord.

18 venues give some buying leverage on beverage and food supply contracts (evidenced by a $1.0m supplier cash payment renegotiated in late 2025), but this is a soft advantage versus true procurement scale.
Hospitality has essentially zero switching costs for the consumer; there is no subscription, loyalty-driven repeat-purchase moat disclosed, and diners can freely substitute to any competing venue.

Individual venue brands (Azabu, Ebisu, MoVida under a licensed partnership with the Melbourne original) carry genuine local reputational equity and awards history, but this is chef/concept-specific rather than a Savor corporate brand halo.

weaknesses: No network effects, no recurring/contracted revenue, and minimal genuine switching costs - a textbook low-moat operating business

High fixed-cost base (rent, IFRS-16 lease commitments, wages) creates severe operating leverage: an 8% revenue decline in FY2025 nearly wiped out earnings, and small swings in trading conditions move NPAT from profit to loss

Single-city (Auckland) concentration means Savor has zero diversification against a local downturn, CBD-specific event (e.g. further lockdowns, construction disruption), or Auckland-specific economic shock

History of goodwill and fixed-asset impairments (FY2024 $4.3m goodwill impairment; FY2025 $1.8m loss on disposal from the discontinued Seafarers fit-out) shows the fragility of individual venue economics
Small absolute scale (~$55m revenue) limits negotiating power against major landlords and national suppliers relative to larger hospitality/retail groups

growth_drivers: Entertainment-format rollout - Flush Golf is trading ahead of expectation with better margins and lower labour intensity than food-led venues; if validated, this format could be replicated at further sites, diversifying the Group away from pure food-and-beverage economics
Margin expansion from continued cost-out - COGS improved to below 28% of revenue and venue wages contributed ~$1m of additional margin in FY26; further overhead and utilities discipline is targeted
Maturation of the two new Britomart venues (Bar Ziti, Flush Golf), opened September 2025, which are still in their first 12 months of trading and expected to contribute more as they mature

First-ever dividend (targeted January 2027, contingent on reaching 1.5x gross leverage, ANZ-approved) could attract a new cohort of income/yield-oriented investors to a stock that has never paid one, potentially re-rating the currently depressed multiple

City Rail Link opening (13 September 2026) and CBD office/foot-traffic recovery (Heart of the City reporting +4% YoY foot traffic to March 2026) - Savor's Britomart cluster sits adjacent to the new Te Waihorotiu station, a potential structural tailwind for CBD dining demand
Ongoing deleveraging (2.4x to 1.92x to 1.8x post April-2026 repayment, ~1.4x net) freeing up cash flow previously consumed by debt service and interest

business.description: Dining out is one of the first categories households cut in a cost-of-living squeeze; FY2025 revenue fell 8% and H1 FY2026 fell 6% amid exactly this pressure.
Over 65% of Group earnings are historically generated in the summer months (roughly Nov-Mar); a poor summer (weather, one-off local event disruption) can determine the entire year's result.

business.risk: Operating leverage / high fixed cost base
business.description: IFRS-16 lease liabilities (~$17-20m across 18 venues) and fixed rent/wage costs mean revenue declines disproportionately hit operating earnings and can flip the Group from profit to loss.
100% of venues are in Auckland with no geographic diversification; any Auckland-specific shock (construction disruption, event cancellations, local economic weakness) hits the whole Group.
Concepts are closely tied to founder-CEO Lucien Law's personal relationships and reputation (e.g. MoVida's Frank Camorra partnership); loss of key chefs or the CEO could damage specific brands.
Hospitality-wide staff shortages and minimum-wage/award inflation have repeatedly pressured margins; historically cited as a top management concern.

NZ hospitality's insolvency rate has run at roughly 3.3x the national business average in 2025-26, with nearly 3,000 hospitality businesses ceasing trading in the past year, evidencing a genuinely difficult operating backdrop even for well-run operators.

financial.description: Gross leverage of 1.92x at 31 March 2026 (1.8x post April repayment) remains a real covenant and interest-cost burden, though materially improved from a $14.6m debt peak in 2021; a 1% rise in interest rates was estimated to move pre-tax earnings by ~$95k-$100k in recent years.

financial.risk: Negative working capital / going concern language
financial.description: The Group has historically run negative working capital (typical for cash-sale hospitality businesses) and covenant-sensitivity commentary features in the accounts every year; management and auditors have concluded going concern is appropriate, but covenant headroom depends on continued trading performance.
The company has never paid a dividend; the promised January 2027 payment is conditional on hitting a 1.5x leverage target and bank approval, and could slip if trading softens.
Only part of historical tax losses are recognised as a deferred tax asset; a return to sustained losses would put this asset (and the associated 'cash equivalent NPAT' framing) at risk.

regulatory.description: Multi-site liquor licensing, health & safety, and local council consent processes create ongoing compliance costs and could constrain or delay new venue openings/renovations.

regulatory.risk: Minimum wage and employment law changes
regulatory.description: As a labour-intensive operator with ~350+ staff, Savor is directly exposed to New Zealand minimum wage increases and other employment cost regulation.

macro.risk: Interest rates and cost-of-living pressure on consumers
macro.description: Elevated NZ interest rates and cost-of-living pressure have directly suppressed discretionary dining spend through FY2025-26; a slower-than-expected easing cycle prolongs the headwind.
Food price inflation (~4.6-4.8% in 2025-26) and general inflation continue to pressure COGS and overheads even as Savor has offset some of this through cost discipline.
While Savor's venues are mainly locals-driven, CBD/Britomart foot traffic benefits from tourism and major-event calendars; a slowdown in visitor arrivals would be a modest incremental headwind.

execution.description: Early results are encouraging but the entertainment format is unproven at scale within the Group; a broader rollout decision would carry real capital and execution risk if replicated to sites where the concept fits less naturally.

execution.risk: Microcap illiquidity and thin free float
execution.description: At ~NZ$0.172/share and ~77.6m shares on issue, market capitalisation is only ~NZ$13m; NZX trading in SVR is very thin, meaning even modest buy/sell orders can move the price materially and large holders cannot easily exit.

The Group has disclosed non-compliance with several NZX Corporate Governance Code recommendations (no majority-independent board, no independent Chair, Audit & Risk Committee not solely non-executive), reflecting the small-cap, founder/Chair-led governance structure.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: The New Zealand hospitality sector is in a genuinely difficult multi-year stretch: close to 3,000 businesses ceased trading in the past year and the industry's insolvency rate has run at roughly 3.3x the national average, driven by input-cost inflation and depressed discretionary consumer spending. Against that backdrop there are tentative green shoots - monthly hospitality spend has ticked up sequentially and Auckland CBD foot traffic was reported up ~4% YoY to March 2026 - but the sector overall remains a 'two-speed' environment favouring premium/experience-led operators (which is where Savor positions itself) over volume-based venues.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High - discretionary consumer spending category, compounded by extreme intra-year seasonality (>65% of earnings concentrated in the Nov-Mar summer period); Savor's earnings have swung from profit to material loss and back within a four-year window (FY2022-FY2026) largely tracking the broader economic cycle.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-to-high, on two fronts: (1) direct - Group borrowings of several million dollars mean NZ OCR/wholesale rate moves flow through interest expense (historically estimated at roughly $95-100k pre-tax earnings impact per 1% rate move); (2) indirect and larger - elevated mortgage and living costs are the primary driver of the discretionary dining pullback the sector has experienced through FY2025-26.
key_input_costs: Food and beverage COGS (protein, seafood, produce, imported beverages)
Labour/wages (largest single cost line, subject to minimum wage and award inflation)
Commercial rent (Auckland CBD/fringe precinct leases, largely fixed under IFRS-16)

recent_developments.event: City Rail Link opens to passengers 13 September 2026, bringing the new Te Waihorotiu station into operation near Savor's Britomart venue cluster; Savor's Annual Shareholders Meeting is also scheduled for September 2026, where an FY27 guidance update is due.

FY2026 annual results released: revenue $55.2m (-2.5%), operating earnings $8.0m (+10%, record 14.5% margin), NPAT $1.3m (vs FY25 loss of $1.2m), EPS 1.7c, leverage down to 1.92x (1.8x post April 2026 repayment); FY27 guidance not reconfirmed pending ASM update, though management separately flagged an FY27 operating-earnings target of $9-10m.
Group repaid a further $0.5m of borrowings, reducing gross leverage from 1.92x to 1.8x; bank borrowings expected to fall to ~$7.5m by end-April 2026 versus a $14.6m peak in 2021.

Management announced Savor is on track to pay its first-ever dividend, targeted at 2 cents per share in January 2027, contingent on reaching 1.5x gross leverage - a target the bank (ANZ) has stress-tested and approved.

H1 FY2026 (six months to 30 September 2025) results: revenue $24.0m (-6%), operating earnings $1.9m (-3%), net loss $1.1m (flat YoY); management renegotiated supplier arrangements generating $1.0m of cash receipts before calendar year end.

Opened two new venues in Britomart's Roukai Lane: Bar Ziti (Italian laneway bar/kitchen) and Flush Golf (5-bay Trackman golf-simulator entertainment venue) - the Group's first entertainment-led concept.
Board Chair Paul Robinson told shareholders at the AGM that he and CEO Lucien Law had voluntarily taken a substantial pay cut, signalling continued cost discipline through the leadership team.

guidance.as_of: FY2026 Annual Results, 26 May 2026 (dividend mechanics per March 2026 announcement)

items.vs_prior: not formally reconfirmed at FY26 result
items.notes: Previously issued FY27 guidance was NOT reconfirmed at the 26 May 2026 result release due to macro uncertainty; management indicated it can 'look through the current instability' given >65% of earnings land in summer, and a formal update is due at the September 2026 ASM. The $9-10m figure has been reported in the financial press as the working FY27 target.

Conditional on Group gross leverage reaching 1.5x, a level the Group's bank (ANZ) has stress-tested and approved for dividend payment; leverage was 1.92x at 31 March 2026 (1.8x post the April 2026 repayment, ~1.4x on a net-debt basis).

items.target: 1.5x gross (bank-approved dividend trigger); net leverage approaching ~0.65x referenced for Q4
items.vs_prior: improving - down from 2.4x (FY25) to 1.92x (FY26) to 1.8x post April 2026 repayment
items.notes: Continued debt paydown is both a balance-sheet and dividend-capacity target; bank borrowings guided toward ~$7.5m by end-April 2026 versus a $14.6m peak in 2021.

items.target: COGS below 28% of revenue maintained or improved; continued venue wage efficiency
items.notes: FY26 COGS improved >1pp to below 28% of revenue and venue wages delivered ~$1m of incremental contribution; management commentary frames further margin gains as achievable through continued overhead and utilities discipline.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Lucien Law: 'FY26 has been a year of tremendous progress for the Group in what's been a tough year for the sector. Revenue softened by under 3%, but Underlying EBITDA lifted 10% and our margin reached a new high. That's the result of consistent discipline at the venue level - and importantly, it's what puts us on track to deliver Savor's first dividend to shareholders.' Management explicitly declined to reconfirm FY27 guidance at the May 2026 result given global economic uncertainty, deferring a formal update to the September 2026 ASM, while noting the extreme seasonal skew toward summer earnings gives visibility to look through near-term instability.

bull_case: First-ever dividend targeted for January 2027 (2 cents/share, ~11-12% of the current ~$0.172 share price) would be a major re-rating catalyst for a stock that has never returned capital to shareholders, potentially attracting income-focused buyers to an otherwise overlooked microcap

Record FY26 operating margin (14.5%) demonstrates genuine, multi-year cost discipline (COGS down >1pp, venue wage efficiency, overhead reduction) that has structurally improved earnings quality even through a revenue downturn

Deleveraging is real and continuing (2.4x to 1.92x to 1.8x, ~1.4x net), materially reducing both financial risk and interest expense drag versus the $14.6m debt peak in 2021, freeing cash flow for shareholders

Flush Golf's early performance (trading ahead of expectation, better margins, lower labour intensity than food-led venues) offers a genuinely differentiated, higher-margin growth format that could be selectively replicated

City Rail Link opening (13 September 2026) directly serves Savor's Britomart venue cluster and coincides with recovering Auckland CBD foot traffic (+4% YoY), a structural tailwind arriving just as the Group's ASM/FY27 guidance update lands

Deep value/microcap mispricing potential - at ~NZ$13m market cap against $55m of revenue and a demonstrated path to $9-10m of FY27 operating earnings, the equity screens statistically cheap if execution continues, though this must be weighed against thin liquidity
bear_case: Structurally low-moat, high-fixed-cost hospitality business: extreme operating leverage means modest revenue softness (as seen in FY2025's 8% decline) can wipe out most of the Group's earnings and flip it back to a net loss

New Zealand hospitality sector backdrop remains genuinely distressed - nearly 3,000 business closures and a 3.3x-average insolvency rate over the past year show Savor is navigating real structural headwinds, not just a temporary soft patch

100% single-city (Auckland) concentration with no geographic diversification leaves the whole Group exposed to any local shock, and >65% of earnings land in a narrow summer window, so a single bad season can derail annual results and the dividend timeline

FY27 guidance was explicitly NOT reconfirmed at the FY26 result due to macro uncertainty - the promised dividend is conditional on hitting a leverage target that itself depends on trading performance holding up, and could slip

Governance concentration (no independent-majority board, no independent Chair, founder-CEO and Chair long-time business partners) plus extremely thin NZX liquidity at a ~NZ$13m market cap mean minority shareholders have limited influence and cannot easily exit a position of any size

History of impairments and one-off write-downs (FY2024 $4.3m goodwill impairment, FY2025 $1.8m Seafarers-related fixed asset loss) shows individual venue economics can deteriorate quickly and unpredictably, and four of the last five fiscal years (FY2022-FY2025) were net losses
